newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees more sports-related brain injuries.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees more sports-related brain injuries.

text.p: Athletes who suffer a seemingly minor concussion and resume playing contact sports before they have fully recovered can die from "second impact syndrome," which is being reported in growing numbers, federal health officials said on Thursday.

The Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said second impact syndrome can occur when a second concussion occurs within hours, days or weeks after the first one. It said the recurrent brain injuries can be serious or fatal.

Researchers estimate there are 300,000 sports-related brain concussions every year. At least 17 cases of second impact syndrome have occurred since 1992, while only four cases were reported between 1984 and 1991, the CDC said.

"We are very concerned about the potential for very severe consequences, even death, if a person suffers a second brain concussion before they have healed from a prior brain concussion," Dr. David Thurman, a medical epidemiologist in the CDC's National Centre for Injury Prevention and Control, said.
Second impact syndrome can occur because of blows to the head in games such as football, hockey, soccer, baseball, basketball and boxing, the CDC said.

The American Academy of Neurology released guidelines on Wednesday urging that athletes who suffer a concussion without losing consciousness be removed from sports activity for a week. Athletes suffering two concussions in one day shouldn't play again for two weeks and those who lose consciousness shouldn't play again for at least a month, the guidelines said.
Second impact syndrome, first recognised in 1984, results from brain swelling that occurs when a second concussion is sustained before complete recovery from a previous concussion.
"Both of those injuries might be mild if considered by themselves, but if they follow too closely, one upon the other, the result can be extremely serious and can result in death," Thurman said.

The CDC cited two examples of deaths from second impact syndrome. One was a 17-year-old high school football player whose head struck the ground when he was tackled during the first half of a varsity game. He told a teammate he felt ill and had a headache but didn't tell his coach. Later in the game, he collapsed on the field and was taken to a hospital in a coma. He was pronounced brain dead four days later.

The other case involved a 19-year-old college football player who complained of a headache after full-contact practice. The following day, he collapsed on the field after engaging in a tackle. He was pronounced brain dead three days later.
